title: Foundations of ML Systems Engineering
oneLiner: Machine learning is one part of a software system built by a team; this session sets out who does what, how ML differs from ordinary code, and the life cycle a model goes through.

what.html:
Software engineering for ML is the craft of turning a trained model into a dependable product. It combines the classic software life cycle (plan, design, build, test, deploy, maintain) with the extra work that data and models bring: collecting and cleaning data, training and versioning models, and watching them in production.

Everyday versionA brilliant recipe (the model) is not a restaurant. You also need suppliers (data pipelines), a kitchen layout (architecture), hygiene checks (testing), opening hours and delivery (deployment), and someone tasting dishes every day to catch problems (monitoring).

why.html:
• Most ML projects fail not because the model is weak but because the system around it is missing or fragile.
  • In ordinary software only the code changes. In ML, the data and the model change too, so there is three times as much to track.
  • You can't write an exact specification for "find the objects in this photo", so ML needs different ways to state and check requirements.
  • Modern AI work is mostly integrating and operating models, which is engineering work.

how.title: The software life cycle and the team
how.html: Software is planned, analysed, designed, built, tested, deployed and maintained, in a loop. A team shares the work: business analysts write requirements, product owners prioritise, architects design, developers build, testers check. Over the decades the way of working moved from waterfall to agile to DevOps and cloud, and now AI helps write documents, code and tests.

how.title: Data people join the team
how.html: Data science turns data into insight and decisions. Data engineers move and store data, data scientists explore it and build models, and ML engineers put models into production, collect the real outcomes and keep the models healthy.

how.title: Build the foundations first
how.html: Data work has a pyramid of needs: collect the data, move and store it, clean it, aggregate and label it, experiment with simple models, and only then reach for advanced AI. Skipping a level makes everything above it shaky.

how.title: Three things change, not one
how.html: A model is learned from data. So besides the code, the data (new months, new sources) and the model (new algorithms, settings) change too. Each change means retesting and re-versioning, and all three must be recorded together to reproduce a result.

how.title: A model's life cycle
how.html: Prepare data, train, evaluate, deploy. Then the important part: monitor the live model, because the world changes and accuracy drifts down, and retrain and release a new version. It's a loop, not a straight line.

how.title: Three generations and four domains
how.html: First we trained small models on labelled data; then deep learning on big data; now we often call huge pre-trained models through an API. Common AI services cover language, speech, vision and decisions (recommendations).

how.title: Foundation models and the AI engineer
how.html: Foundation models (large language models are the best-known kind) are trained once on huge amounts of data and adapted to many tasks. The AI engineer who builds with them needs software skills first: Python, APIs, Git, CI/CD, plus RAG, prompting and fine-tuning.

how.title: Why ML can't be specified like normal code
how.html: "Compute tax deductions" can be described exactly. "Detect the objects in this picture" can't. ML replaces exact rules with examples and acceptable error rates, and replaces "is it correct?" with "how accurate is it?".

demo.html: You are the loan officer. Drag the sliders to write your own approval rule and watch the accuracy. Then press Learn the rule from data and compare. Increase the noise: hand-written rules get harder to tune, which is exactly when learning from data pays off.

example.html:
Churn model at a telecom company. A data engineer builds the pipeline that collects call and billing records; a data scientist trains a churn model (F1 0.81); an ML engineer deploys it behind an API for the CRM, logs every prediction and who actually left. Three months later a competitor's cheaper plan changes customer behaviour, live F1 drops to 0.66, monitoring raises an alert, and the model is retrained and released as version 2.

Supplementary The same story with a foundation model: a support chatbot built on an LLM API has no training step, but still needs prompt versioning, evaluation, cost limits and monitoring.

misunderstandings: Once the model is accurate, the job is done.
Accuracy is the start. The model must be served, monitored and retrained as data changes.
ML engineers and data scientists do the same thing.
Data scientists mostly explore and build models; ML engineers make them run reliably in production.
Calling an LLM API means no engineering is needed.
You still need integration, evaluation, cost control, privacy and monitoring.
You also need the data snapshot and the model settings to reproduce a result.
You can't have requirements for ML.
You can: goals, metrics, acceptable error rates and data requirements (Session M3).
takeaways: The SDLC (plan → maintain) and its roles still apply to ML projects; ML adds data and model work.
Data engineers move data, data scientists build models, ML engineers run and maintain them in production.
Build the data hierarchy of needs from the bottom: collect, store, clean, label, experiment, then AI.
ML has three axes of change (code, data, model) and a model life cycle that loops: develop, version, deploy, monitor, retrain.
ML behaviour can't be specified exactly; it is specified by examples and measured by accuracy rather than functional correctness.
thirty: Software engineering for ML treats the model as one component of a larger system built by a team. The usual life cycle still applies, with business analysts, architects, developers and testers, and data roles join it: data engineers build pipelines, data scientists build models, and ML engineers run them in production. Data work follows a hierarchy: collect, store, clean, label, experiment, and only then advanced AI. Unlike ordinary software, three things change: code, data and model, so all three must be versioned together. A model's life is a loop of develop, version, deploy, monitor and retrain. Today many systems use foundation models through APIs, which moves effort from training to integration. And because we can't write an exact specification for tasks like object detection, ML is specified by examples and judged by accuracy.
